Havelock Ellis, an English writer on psychology and society, published these essays during the First World War. He asks how war changes nations: their birth rates, their morals, their democracies, and their ideas about men, women, and health.

Chapters weigh whether war is fading, what it does to family life, and how a country might organize health and ability in peacetime. Ellis writes plainly and argues from evidence rather than slogans. The essays give a thoughtful, wartime view of social reform that still reads as serious public argument for readers today.
essays-in-war-time-further-studies-in-th:
Havelock Ellis turns his science on the Great War in Essays in War-Time, further studies in the task of social hygiene. Eighteen chapters ask whether war is diminishing, what it does to the birth-rate, and how it touches democracy. War and eugenics, morality in warfare, and the mental differences of men and women fill the first half.

Ellis splits the common claim that war preserves human virtue into three separate propositions, refusing to affirm them wholesale. Later chapters take the white slave crusade, the conquest of venereal disease, and the nationalisation of health. Footnotes cite the British Medical Journal of February 5th, 1916, on syphilis and progeny. Marriage, divorce, and birth control close a book that treats war as a public-health problem.

Comedian and jiu-jitsu coach Eddie Bravo shares his take on the new UFO whistleblower in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Bravo, Rogan's longtime friend, is famous on the show for embracing the wildest reading of any story. Rogan lets him build the case his way.

Bravo walks through what the whistleblower claimed and why he finds it convincing. Rogan plays the mildly saner friend, asking where the proof sits. The segment is less a briefing than a show of the pair's dynamic: one man chasing the fringe at full speed, the other half a step behind, laughing and listening.

Scholar Alan Levinovitz joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1504 to talk about food myths. Levinovitz studies how health fads dress themselves in the language of religion and purity. His book on the subject treats gluten panic as a case study in modern belief.

He and Rogan pick apart the rules people swear by, from clean eating to miracle diets, and ask what proof sits under each one. Rogan brings the gym world's habits into the dock as well. The episode is a calm debunking session that still respects why food rules feel so powerful to the people who live by them.
